question.value: Whether the SiO maser stars around Sagittarius A* are members of the Nuclear Star Cluster (NSC) or the Nuclear Stellar Disk (NSD) based on statistical properties of their 3D kinematics.

evidence.quote: However, these studies implicitly assume that these maser stars are members of the NSC only because they are observed in the direction of the NSC.
Here we focus on resolving this question based on statistical properties in the kinematics of SiO maser stars.
These results indicate that the SiO maser stars are members of the NSD rather than the NSC.

claims.hypothesis: SiO maser stars observed in the direction of Sgr A* have randomized proper motion position angles similar to the early-type (WR and O) stars in the Nuclear Star Cluster (NSC).
claims.experiment: Derive the proper motions relative to Sgr A* for 35 SiO maser stars between 2017 and 2021 using ALMA SiO v=1, J=2-1 astrometry and compare their position angle histogram to that of WR and O stars in the NSC.
claims.result: The position angle distribution of the SiO maser stars is bipolar with peaks coinciding with the direction of the Galactic plane, whereas the NSC early-type stars show a random distribution.
claims.finding: The statistical property of the proper motions of SiO maser stars is different from that of the NSC, showing a tendency to lie along the Galactic plane consistent with the Nuclear Stellar Disk (NSD).

evidence.loc: 4.1 Proper motion along the Galactic plane
evidence.quote: The distribution of the position angles are bipolar rather than random. The black arrows indicate the direction of the Galactic plane. The peaks of the distribution coincide with the direction of the Galactic plane.

evidence.loc: 4.1 Proper motion along the Galactic plane
evidence.quote: It is therefore plausible that the statistical property of the proper motions of the SiO maser stars is different from that of the NSC.

claims.hypothesis: The SiO maser stars around Sgr A* are members of the Nuclear Stellar Disk (NSD) passing in front of or behind Sgr A* on larger-radius orbits rather than randomized members of the NSC.
claims.experiment: Compare the mean proper motion speed amplitude |V_prop| and mean LSR radial velocity amplitude |V_LSR| of the SiO maser stars, and compare their 3D space velocities V_space = sqrt(V_prop^2 + V_LSR^2) against Keplerian orbital velocity limits around Sgr A* (M = 4 x 10^6 M_sun).
claims.result: |V_prop| = 153.2 +- 83.3 km s^-1 is much larger than |V_LSR| = 66.1 +- 60.6 km s^-1, and many 3D space velocities exceed the circular Keplerian velocity sqrt(GM/r) and reach or exceed the parabolic limit sqrt(2GM/r).
claims.finding: The dominance of transverse motion along the Galactic plane and 3D space velocities near or above the Keplerian escape limit indicate that the SiO maser stars around Sgr A* belong to the NSD rather than the NSC.

evidence.loc: 4.2 Disproportionate proper motion speed and LSR speed

why_this_data.value: ALMA has a sharp synthesized beam, high sensitivity, a large FOV (67.5'' FWHM at 86.2 GHz), and simultaneously detects Sgr A* in continuum so star positions can be directly referenced to Sgr A* while radial velocities are easily obtained from the SiO maser line.

evidence.quote: The radial velocity of the maser star is easily observable, but that of the early-type stars is not easy to infer. ALMA has a very sharp synthesized beam with very high sensitivity.
Moreover, the position of the stars can be measured directly by referencing the position of Sgr A

why_this_method.value: Velocity integration width was set to 5 km s^-1 to improve sensitivity for detecting fainter stars and increase the sample size for statistical kinematics, and outer FOV limit was extended to primary beam attenuation of 0.2.

The outer limit of the FOV was set so that the attenuation by the primary beam pattern of the 12 m antenna is 0.2 because the ALMA has high sensitivity.

referee_caveats_inferred: Selection bias against high radial velocities or weak masers at large radii due to the primary beam cutoff (0.2) and velocity range (-350 to +350 km/s) is not modeled quantitatively.

Statistical claims (bipolar PA distribution, velocity comparisons) rely on visual inspection of histograms and simple means/standard deviations of 35 stars without formal statistical hypothesis tests (e.g., KS test against uniform or NSC distributions).
Potential astrometric shift from changing maser spot distributions within the stellar circumstellar shell between 2017 and 2021 is not quantified.
